<Rep. Robert C. "Bobby" Scott>: Despite this history of working in a bipartisan manner, the Majority has regrettably chosen to advance H.R. 7895 through a partisan process and without input from Democrat Members. As a result, the bill fails to fully advance a comprehensive policy that addresses the needs of workers and employers alike. H.R. 7895's deficiencies could have been addressed had the Majority chosen to engage in a deliberate, bipartisan process.
This legislation seeks to address the single PBM business practice of referral fees paid by PBMs to certain brokers and consultants that create an incentive to steer clients to those same PBMs. Unfortunately, the introduced version of the legislation was flawed in addressing even this limited issue. For example, rather than encompass the wide range of ways in which PBMs could structure or characterize such payments to brokers and consultants, the bill instead relies upon the undefined concept of ``referral'' of a client's business to a PBM. Experts noted that this would allow PBMs and brokers, consultants, and similar entities to simply characterize these payments as something else, such as a ``consulting service'' or another label, and evade the bill's prohibition entirely.\27\ Fortunately, this particular deficiency was corrected through last minute changes to the text in the Amendment in the Nature of a Substitute (ANS).
\27\Terence Park et al., The PBM Kickback Prohibition Act: Well- Intentioned but Potentially Ineffective Reform, Frier Levitt (Apr. 3, 2026), https://www.frierlevitt.com/articles/pbm-kickback-prohibition-act-erisa-plan-sponsors/.
However, even with this change in the ANS, the Majority's exclusive focus on PBMs falls short of addressing the scope of the problem facing workers and employers. As noted previously, it has been documented that brokers and consultants receive payments from service providers other than PBMs, including insurers and third party administrators, that steer employers to such service providers.\28\ The Committee understood this fact when advancing the Ban Surprise Billing Act on a bipartisan basis.\29\ That bill improved transparency with respect to such payments in the form of compensation received from ``any [indirect] source'' and certain provisions were enacted into law in the CAA 2021.\30\ Regrettably, H.R. 7895 fails to incorporate this previous bipartisan approach to address a much broader problem and instead only proposes to prohibit these payments with respect to PBMs.
\28\See Allen, supra note 20.
\29\Ban Surprise Billing Act, H.R. 5800, 116th Cong. (2020).
\30\29 U.S.C. Sec. 1108(b)(2)(B)(ii)(dd)(CC).
The Majority has not provided a satisfactory explanation for this approach. During the Markup of H.R. 7895, Rep. DeSaulnier expressed concern that the bill's narrow scope failed to address compensation received from other service providers that present a potential conflict of interest.\31\ He offered an amendment that would have ensured that the kickback prohibition applies to all covered service providers described in section 408(b)(2) of ERISA, consistent with the Committee's past, bipartisan approach. In opposing the amendment, Health, Employment, Labor, and Pensions Subcommittee Chair Rick Allen (R-GA) offered no substantive explanation for the Majority's position. In fact, he seemed to concede that the issue remains unaddressed by H.R. 7895 but noted that, rather than tackle this problem, the Committee should defer to the policy wishes of the Trump White House, stating:
\31\Comm. on Educ. and Workforce Democrats, Markup: H.R. 8736, H.R. 8705, H.R. 7362, H.R. 7895, H.R. 8684, YouTube at 2:42:47 (May 21, 2026), https://youtu.be/o_KSOp_SvLI.
Cracking down on PBMs paying kickbacks to consultants
and brokers is a key feature of President Trump's
``Great Healthcare Plan.'' Other entities may also be
making steering payments to brokers and consultants.
However, to address PBMs' pharmaceutical monopoly we
must keep the scope of this bill focused on PBMs to
lower costs as part of the President's ``Great
Healthcare Plan.''\32\
\32\Id. at 2:45:33.
It is regrettable that the Majority would defer to a 22-word bullet point contained in President Trump's so-called ``Great Healthcare Plan,''\33\ rather than develop legislation that meets the needs of the American people.
\33\Supra note 2.
CONCLUSION
Addressing the growing cost of health care in the United States requires legislation that results in reforms that meaningfully address the problems presented. Committee Democrats supported H.R. 7895 because it represents a small step toward addressing misaligned incentives and improving employer-sponsored health care. However, the legislation should be improved to ensure that it meaningfully addresses the full scope of conflicts of interest among health plan service providers such as insurance companies, third party administrators, and other middlemen. Moving forward, the Committee should work to advance legislation that goes beyond the narrow scope of H.R. 7895 and consider these important issues in a more comprehensive manner. I hope the Majority will work with us to improve H.R. 7895 as it moves forward in the House.
Robert C. ``Bobby'' Scott,
Ranking Member.
